title: Hypoglycaemia in hospital
blurb: Treat hypoglycaemia in hospital the JBDS way: pick the right algorithm for the person's conscious level, recheck on time, follow up, and keep the next insulin dose.
question: Mrs Nakamura, 70, has type 2 diabetes on insulin. At 11:00 her capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. She is alert, orientated and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?

teach.body: In hospital, hypoglycaemia is a blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L in an adult with diabetes, with or without symptoms. JBDS says treat it as an emergency whatever the conscious level. If the reading is above 4.0 but the person has symptoms, a small carbohydrate snack relieves them. Plain English: any reading below 4.0 is treated now, even if the person says they feel fine.

teach.h: Choose the algorithm by conscious level

root.label: CBG below 4.0 mmol/L
root.sub: Quick ABCDE; stop any IV insulin infusion

children.label: 2 tubes 40% glucose gel
children.sub: Glucagon 1 mg IM if gel ineffective

children.label: Call for help; IV glucose
children.sub: Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV access

teach.caption: Glucose gel goes between the teeth and gums. Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person.

teach.h: The treatment cycle (alert and able to swallow)

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Still below 4.0 after 30–45 min or 3 cycles

teach.caption: Escalation options: glucagon 1 mg IM, or IV 100 mL of 20% glucose or 200 mL of 10% glucose over 15 minutes.

teach.h: After the hypo: snack, insulin and monitoring
teach.body: Once glucose is above 4.0 and the person has recovered, give 20 g long-acting carbohydrate, such as two biscuits, a slice of bread, 200–300 mL milk (not soya or alternative milks), or their meal if due. After glucagon, give 40 g to restore glycogen. Do not omit the next insulin injection: it is unlikely to be the dose that caused the hypo, though the regimen needs review. Find the cause and record the event.

teach.text: Two classic errors: skipping the next insulin dose 'to be safe', and starting a variable rate insulin infusion to 'stabilise' glucose. JBDS says do neither. Omitting insulin in type 1 diabetes risks DKA. Also: 40 g follow-up is for after glucagon, 20 g otherwise.

rows.label: Use when
values: No IV access, or gel ineffective

rows.label: Caution
values: Weaker with sulfonylureas, alcohol, liver disease

teach.caption: Glucagon releases liver glycogen, so it works poorly in malnutrition, prolonged starvation, alcohol misuse or chronic liver disease.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Farah on the surgical ward
teach.body: Mr Farah, 58, takes gliclazide and has eaten little since surgery. At 16:00 his glucose is 2.9 and he is muddled and won't take tablets, but can swallow. The nurse squeezes 2 tubes of 40% glucose gel between his teeth and gums and rechecks after 10–15 minutes: 4.6. He then eats a sandwich. Because sulfonylurea hypos can recur for 24–36 hours, she continues regular glucose checks and asks for the gliclazide to be reviewed.

teach.caption: JBDS also advises considering intervention at a CBG below 6.0 in most people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, to prevent a hypo.

items: Below 4.0 mmol/L is hypoglycaemia; treat it whether or not there are symptoms.
Alert: 15–20 g fast carbohydrate, recheck in 10–15 min, up to 3 cycles, then escalate.
Confused but swallowing: 2 tubes 40% glucose gel; glucagon 1 mg IM if the gel is ineffective.
Unconscious: ABCDE, call for help, IV glucose (glucagon IM if no access); stop any insulin infusion.
Then 20 g long-acting carbohydrate (40 g after glucagon), and do not omit the next insulin.

summary: You can now recognise hypoglycaemia in hospital, choose the JBDS treatment for the person's conscious level, and recheck and escalate on time. You can also give the right follow-up carbohydrate, keep the next insulin dose and look for the cause.

A.q: Mrs Nakamura, 70, on insulin, has a capillary glucose of 3.1 mmol/L. She is alert, orientated and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?
options: Two digestive biscuits and a cup of tea
A.why: JBDS 01 algorithm A: for an adult who is conscious, orientated and able to swallow, give 15–20 g rapid-acting carbohydrate (for example 150–200 mL pure fruit juice or 5–7 glucose tablets).

whyNot.0: Biscuits are long-acting carbohydrate given after glucose is above 4.0, not the first treatment.
whyNot.2: Glucagon is for when oral treatment has failed or cannot be given; she can swallow.
whyNot.3: IV glucose is for people who are unconscious or not responding to oral treatment.

A.q: After treating a hypoglycaemic episode with oral glucose, when should the nurse recheck the capillary blood glucose?
A.why: JBDS 01: repeat the capillary blood glucose 10–15 minutes after each treatment.

whyNot.0: 30–45 minutes is the point at which to call for help if glucose is still low, not the first recheck.
whyNot.1: Waiting until a meal could leave the person hypoglycaemic for hours.
whyNot.2: 60 minutes is too long to leave a possible ongoing hypo.

A.q: Mr Ruiz has chronic kidney disease and follows a low-potassium diet. He has a hypo at 3.4 mmol/L and is alert. Which treatment should the nurse avoid?
A.why: JBDS 01: do not use pure fruit juice for people on a low-potassium diet (for example in CKD) because of its potassium content.

whyNot.0: Glucose tablets are suitable and potassium-free.
whyNot.1: The juice shot is a measured glucose product listed by JBDS as suitable.
whyNot.3: Sugar in water is suitable unless the person takes acarbose.

B.q: Mr Farah, 58, has a glucose of 2.9 mmol/L. He is confused and refusing tablets but can swallow. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Wait until he is calmer, then retest
Ask him to drink a carton of milk
Start a variable rate insulin infusion
B.why: JBDS 01 algorithm B: if the person is not capable or cooperative but can swallow, give 2 tubes of 40% glucose gel between the teeth and gums, or glucagon 1 mg IM if this is ineffective.

whyNot.1: Delay prolongs neuroglycopenia; treatment is needed now.
whyNot.2: Milk is a follow-up long-acting carbohydrate, and he is refusing oral intake.
whyNot.3: Insulin would lower glucose further and is contraindicated during a hypo.

B.q: Mrs Begum's hypoglycaemia was treated with glucagon 1 mg IM. She is now awake and her glucose is 5.2 mmol/L. What follow-up carbohydrate does JBDS advise?
options: No snack, as glucagon lasts several hours
A further 15–20 g of glucose tablets
B.why: JBDS 01: people given glucagon need a larger portion of long-acting carbohydrate (40 g) to replenish glycogen stores.

whyNot.0: 20 g is the standard follow-up when glucagon was not used.
whyNot.1: Glucagon has used up liver glycogen; without a snack, glucose may fall again.
whyNot.3: Glucose is already above 4.0; she needs long-acting, not more rapid-acting, carbohydrate.

B.q: Mr Lowe, who has type 1 diabetes, had a hypo at 07:30 that has been treated. His glucose is now 6.8 mmol/L and his breakfast insulin is due at 08:00. What should the nurse do?
options: Omit the 08:00 dose to prevent another hypo
Give the dose and arrange a regimen review
Halve the dose without discussing it
Start a variable rate insulin infusion
B.why: JBDS 01: do not omit an insulin injection if due; it is unlikely to be the dose that caused the hypo. Review the insulin regimen. Omitting insulin in type 1 diabetes risks DKA.

whyNot.0: JBDS specifically says do not omit the next insulin dose.
whyNot.2: Dose changes need a prescriber or diabetes team decision, not a unilateral cut.
whyNot.3: JBDS advises against starting a VRIII to 'stabilise' glucose after a hypo.

C.q: Mrs Achebe, 77, is unconscious with a glucose of 1.9 mmol/L. She has no IV access and the doctor is on the way. She takes glibenclamide and drinks heavily. After calling for help, what should the nurse do?
options: Give glucose gel into her mouth
Glucagon 1 mg IM; keep trying for IV access
Wait for the doctor to site a cannula
Give 150 mL fruit juice via a syringe
C.why: JBDS 01 algorithm C: if no IV access, give glucagon 1 mg IM, but keep trying for IV access because glucagon is less effective with sulfonylureas, alcohol misuse or liver disease, and IV glucose is preferred.

whyNot.0: Nothing is given by mouth to an unconscious person: aspiration risk.
whyNot.2: Waiting delays treatment of a life-threatening hypo; glucagon should be given now.
whyNot.3: Oral fluids are unsafe when unconscious.

C.q: Mr Bianchi has had three treatments of 15–20 g glucose over 40 minutes. He is alert but his glucose remains 3.3 mmol/L. What should the nurse do next?
options: Give a fourth oral treatment and recheck in an hour
Give a sandwich and recheck at teatime
Call for medical help; consider IV glucose or glucagon
Record it and recheck at the next routine round
C.why: JBDS 01: if glucose remains below 4.0 after 30–45 minutes or 3 treatment cycles, call for medical assistance and consider glucagon 1 mg IM or IV 20% or 10% glucose over 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: JBDS limits oral treatment to 3 cycles before escalating.
whyNot.1: A sandwich is follow-up once glucose is above 4.0, not treatment of an ongoing hypo.
whyNot.3: Leaving a persistent hypo until a routine round is unsafe.

C.q: Mrs Kelly is on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion. Her glucose is 3.5 mmol/L and she is alert. What should the nurse do first about the infusion?
options: Halve the rate and recheck in 1 hour
Continue it and give glucose tablets
Stop it and switch to subcutaneous insulin
Stop it now, treat, then restart once treated
C.why: JBDS 01: if an insulin infusion is running, stop it immediately, treat the hypo, and restart it once the hypo has been fully treated, reviewing the dose.

whyNot.0: Insulin continues to lower glucose; it must be stopped, not reduced.
whyNot.1: Continuing insulin while treating opposes the treatment.
whyNot.2: JBDS restarts the infusion after treatment and review; it does not switch route.

reteach.title: Traffic lights for hypos
reteach.question: JBDS summarises its algorithms like traffic lights. Which treatment goes with which colour?

blocks.body: Green: alert and can swallow. Give 15–20 g fast carbohydrate, recheck in 10–15 minutes, repeat up to 3 times. Amber: conscious but confused or uncooperative, can swallow. Give 2 tubes of glucose gel, then glucagon IM if the gel is ineffective. Red: unconscious, fitting or very aggressive. Call for help, IV glucose, glucagon IM if no access. Every colour: stop any insulin infusion, then follow up with long-acting carbohydrate and keep the next insulin.

bands.label: Confused: glucose gel or glucagon IM

blocks.text: The follow-up snack is 20 g, or 40 g after glucagon. And the next insulin dose is given, not skipped.

explain.body: Blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L in an adult with diabetes in hospital, with or without symptoms. Symptomatic above 4.0: give a small carbohydrate snack.

test.q: A man on insulin feels shaky and sweaty. His glucose is 4.6 mmol/L. What does JBDS advise?
options: No action as he is above 4.0
test.why: JBDS 01: if glucose is not below 4.0 but the person is symptomatic, give a small carbohydrate snack for symptom relief.

whyNot.0: The full hypo algorithm starts below 4.0 mmol/L.
whyNot.3: He has symptoms, so a snack is advised.

explain.body: 15–20 g rapid-acting carbohydrate of the person's choice, recheck in 10–15 minutes, up to 3 treatments. Still below 4.0 after 30–45 minutes or 3 cycles: call for medical help.

test.q: Which of these provides about 15–20 g of rapid-acting carbohydrate?
test.why: JBDS 01 lists 150–200 mL pure fruit juice (not on a low-potassium diet) as a rapid-acting treatment.

whyNot.1: Toast is long-acting carbohydrate for follow-up.
whyNot.2: Milk (and not soya) is a follow-up option, not rapid-acting treatment.

explain.body: Confused but swallowing: 2 tubes 40% glucose gel between teeth and gums, or glucagon 1 mg IM if the gel is ineffective. Unconscious: ABCDE, call for help, IV 100 mL 20% or 200 mL 10% glucose over 15 minutes, or glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV access.

test.q: What volume of 20% glucose does JBDS use intravenously for severe hypoglycaemia?
test.why: JBDS 01: 100 mL of 20% glucose (or 200 mL of 10%) over 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: JBDS does not use a 50 mL rapid bolus of 20% glucose.
whyNot.1: 500 mL over an hour is far more volume and too slow.
whyNot.2: 200 mL over 15 minutes is the 10% glucose regimen.

explain.body: Above 4.0 and recovered: 20 g long-acting carbohydrate (40 g after glucagon). Do not omit the next insulin. Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin hypos can recur for 24–36 hours, so keep monitoring and find the cause.

test.q: A woman's hypo was caused by gliclazide. For how long does JBDS warn that the risk may persist?
test.why: JBDS 01: if hypoglycaemia was caused by a sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin, the risk may persist for up to 24–36 hours after the last dose, especially with renal impairment.

whyNot.1: Sulfonylurea effects last much longer than 2 hours.
whyNot.2: One meal does not remove the drug's ongoing effect.
whyNot.3: 7 days overstates the JBDS warning period.
